# Cakkavākajātaka (Ja 434)

**ID:** Ja 434  
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Cakkavākajātaka  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul8.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul8.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cakkavākajātaka* (Ja 434) is a canonical birth story preserved in the Jātaka collection of the Pali Canon. Set while the Buddha was residing at Jetavana, the story was occasioned by a greedy monk (*lolabhikkhu*) who was insatiable regarding material requisites [Fausböll 1883]. In relating the past story, the narrative recounts the dialogue between a crow and a ruddy goose (*cakkavāka*, the Bodhisatta) residing with his mate in a lotus lake, contrasting the crow's scavenging diet with the virtuous restraint and mutual devotion of the geese [Fausböll 1883]. At the conclusion of the sermon, after the declaration of the Four Noble Truths, the greedy monk attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), and the characters of the past are identified: the crow was the greedy monk, the female goose was Rāhulamātā, and the male goose was the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1883]. In secondary scholarship on the Buddha legend, the text is cited for the Buddha instructing his disciples on the four foundations of mindfulness, the Noble Eightfold Path, and nine transcendent conditions that overcome Māra [Khosla 1989].

**Sources**

- [Fausböll 1883] V. Fausböll, The Jātaka together with its Commentary, Vol. 3 (1883) — Supplies the Pali text of Ja 434, including the opening nidāna, commentary on the verse, and conclusion with identification of characters.
- [Khosla 1989] Sarla Khosla, Historical Evolution of the Buddha Legend (1989) — Discusses Ja 434 in connection with overcoming Māra.
